claim: Ca2+-stimulated translocation of cytosolic phospholipase A2α (cPLA2α) to the Golgi induces arachidonic acid production.
source: Ca2+-stimulated translocation of cytosolic phospholipase A2α (cPLA2α) to the Golgi induces arachidonic acid production, the rate-limiting step in pro-inflammatory eicosanoid synthesis.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: Arachidonic acid production is the rate-limiting step in pro-inflammatory eicosanoid synthesis.
source: Ca2+-stimulated translocation of cytosolic phospholipase A2α (cPLA2α) to the Golgi induces arachidonic acid production, the rate-limiting step in pro-inflammatory eicosanoid synthesis.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and is supported by established knowledge in the field.

claim: The structure of the cPLA2α C2-domain bound to DHPC and Ca2+ ions was determined at 2.2 Å resolution.
source: Here, we report the structure of the cPLA2α C2-domain (at 2.2 Å resolution), which contains bound 1,2-dihexanoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DHPC) and Ca2+ ions.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Two Ca2+ ions are complexed at previously reported locations in the lipid-free C2-domain.
source: Two Ca2+ are complexed at previously reported locations in the lipid-free C2-domain.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by comparison with previous structural studies.

claim: One Ca2+ ion, along with a third Ca2+, bridges the C2-domain to the DHPC phosphate group.
source: One of these Ca2+ions, along with a third Ca2+, bridges the C2-domain to the DHPC phosphate group, which also interacts with Asn65.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by structural data showing Ca2+ coordination.

claim: The DHPC phosphate group interacts with Asn65.
source: One of these Ca2+ions, along with a third Ca2+, bridges the C2-domain to the DHPC phosphate group, which also interacts with Asn65.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by structural data.

claim: Tyr96 plays a key role in lipid headgroup recognition via cation–π interaction with the PC trimethylammonium group.
source: Tyr96 plays a key role in lipid headgroup recognition via cation–π interaction with the PC trimethylammonium group.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by structural and mutagenesis data.

claim: Mutagenesis analyses confirm that Tyr96 and Asn65 function in PC binding selectivity by the C2-domain.
source: Mutagenesis analyses confirm that Tyr96 and Asn65 function in PC binding selectivity by the C2-domain and in the regulation of cPLA2α activity.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by mutagenesis experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Tyr96 and Asn65 function in the regulation of cPLA2α activity.
source: Mutagenesis analyses confirm that Tyr96 and Asn65 function in PC binding selectivity by the C2-domain and in the regulation of cPLA2α activity.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by activity assays presented in the manuscript.

claim: The DHPC-binding mode of the cPLA2α C2-domain differs from phosphatidylserine or phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate binding by other C2-domains.
source: The DHPC-binding mode of the cPLA2α C2-domain, which differs from phosphatidylserine or phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate binding by other C2-domains, expands and deepens knowledge of the lipid-binding mechanisms mediated by C2-domains.
evidence: This claim is stated in the abstract and supported by structural comparisons with other C2-domains.

claim: Phospholipase A2 (PLA2) hydrolyzes the sn-2 acyl bond of glycerol-based phospholipids.
source: Phospholipase A2 (PLA2) is a member of a diverse enzyme superfamily that hydrolyzes the sn-2 acyl bond of glycerol-based phospholipids (Smith, 1989; Dennis et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cytosolic PLA2α (cPLA2α) preferentially releases arachidonic acid from PLs in a cytosolic Ca2+-concentration-dependent manner.
source: Cytosolic PLA2α (cPLA2α), a Group IV mammalian PLA2 family member, preferentially releases arachidonic acid from PLs in a cytosolic Ca2+-concentration-dependent manner (Clark et al., 1991; Shimizu et al., 2006; Leslie et al., 2010; Vasquez et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Arachidonic acid generated by cPLA2α is a precursor of pro-inflammatory eicosanoids, including certain prostaglandins and leukotrienes.
source: Arachidonic acid generated by cPLA2α is a precursor of pro-inflammatory eicosanoids, including certain prostaglandins and leukotrienes.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and is supported by established biochemical knowledge.

claim: cPLA2-mediated bioactive lipid production plays a major regulatory role in physiological and pathogenic processes.
source: Consequently, cPLA2-mediated bioactive lipid production plays a major regulatory role in physiological and pathogenic processes (Bonventre et al., 1997; Uozumi et al., 1997; Leslie, 2015).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Arachidonic acid release by cPLA2α at the membrane surface is the rate-limiting step in eicosanoid production.
source: Insights into cPLA2α activation by regulatory mediators are of great importance because arachidonic acid release by cPLA2α at the membrane surface is the rate-limiting step in eicosanoid production.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and is supported by established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Prostaglandin production occurs via cyclooxygenases.
source: The ensuing prostaglandin and leukotriene production occurs via cyclooxygenases and lipoxygenases, respectively.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and is supported by established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Leukotriene production occurs via lipoxygenases.
source: The ensuing prostaglandin and leukotriene production occurs via cyclooxygenases and lipoxygenases, respectively.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and is supported by established biochemical knowledge.

claim: Increases in intracellular Ca2+ concentration induced by extracellular stimuli activate cPLA2α by inducing translocation from the cytoplasm to the perinuclear region.
source: Increases in intracellular Ca2+ concentration that are induced by extracellular stimuli activate cPLA2α by inducing translocation from the cytoplasm to the perinuclear region, (i.e. the Golgi apparatus, nuclear envelope and endoplasmic reticulum) (Evans et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The membrane translocation of cPLA2α is driven primarily by its N–terminal C2-domain rather than its catalytic domain.
source: Mechanistically, the membrane translocation of cPLA2α is driven primarily by its N–terminal C2-domain rather than its catalytic domain (Nalefski et al., 1994; Davletov et al., 1998; Dessen et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Complexation of two Ca2+ ions by the C2-domain neutralizes several Asp residues, facilitating protein docking and penetration into the membrane interface region.
source: Complexation of two Ca2+ ions by the C2-domain neutralizes several Asp residues, facilitating protein docking and penetration into the membrane interface region (Davletov et al., 1998; Dessen et al., 1999; Perisic et al., 1998; Bittova et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Occupation of one Ca2+-binding site exerts stronger effects than occupation of the other in terms of stabilizing the membrane partitioning of the cPLA2α C2-domain.
source: Occupation of one Ca2+-binding site exerts stronger effects than occupation of the other in terms of stabilizing the membrane partitioning of the cPLA2α C2-domain (Bittova et al., 1999; Stahelin and Cho, 2001a).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Ceramide-1-phosphate (C1P) enhances enzyme translocation to perinuclear regions by binding directly to the C2-domain.
source: Mutational functional analyses have revealed that ceramide-1-phosphate (C1P), a bioactive sphingolipid generated by ceramide kinase in the trans-Golgi, enhances enzyme translocation to perinuclear regions (Pettus et al., 2004; Stahelin et al., 2007; Lamour et al., 2009) by binding directly to the C2-domain.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2) activates cPLA2α independently of intracellular Ca2+ concentration.
source: Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2) also activates cPLA2α, but independently of intracellular Ca2+ concentration (Mosior et al., 1998; Das and Cho, 2002; Casas et al., 2006), by binding a site that is enriched in cationic residues in the catalytic domain (Das and Cho, 2002; Six and Dennis, 2003; Tucker et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: PI(4,5)P2 binds a site that is enriched in cationic residues in the catalytic domain of cPLA2α.
source: Phosphatidylinositol 4,5-bisphosphate (PI(4,5)P2) also activates cPLA2α, but independently of intracellular Ca2+ concentration (Mosior et al., 1998; Das and Cho, 2002; Casas et al., 2006), by binding a site that is enriched in cationic residues in the catalytic domain (Das and Cho, 2002; Six and Dennis, 2003; Tucker et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The cationic residue clusters that the cPLA2α C2-domain uses to bind C1P for membrane targeting differ from those used by other C2-domains that bind PI(4,5)P2.
source: The cationic residue clusters that the cPLA2α C2-domain uses to bind C1P for membrane targeting (Stahelin et al., 2007; Ward et al., 2013) differ from those used by other C2-domains [e.g., protein kinase C (PKC), Syt and Rabphilin] that bind PI(4,5)P2 (Honigmann et al., 2013; Guillén et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: NMR data have enabled the identification of several residues in the C2-domain calcium binding loops (CBLs) that interact with dodecylphosphocholine micelles.
source: NMR data have enabled the identification of several residues in the C2-domain calcium binding loops (CBLs) that interact with dodecylphosphocholine micelles (Xu et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry and molecular dynamic studies have helped to map the membrane interaction regions of the C2-domain.
source: Hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry and molecular dynamic studies have also helped to map the membrane interaction regions of the C2-domain and have shed light on catalytic domain conformational accommodation of methyl arachidonoyl fluorophosphonate, a cPLA2α active-site inhibitor and 1-palmitoyl-2-arachidonoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (PAPC) substrate (Burke et al., 2008; Cao et al., 2013; Mouchlis et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The lack of crystal structures for the cPLA2α C2-domain or for the cPLA2α catalytic domain containing bound phosphoglyceride has hampered understanding of the structural basis that underlies the lipid activation mechanism(s) and the known preference of cPLA2 for phosphatidylcholine (PC)-enriched membranes.
source: Nonetheless, the lack of crystal structures for the cPLA2α C2-domain or for the cPLA2α catalytic domain containing bound phosphoglyceride has hampered understanding of the structural basis that underlies the lipid activation mechanism(s) and the known preference of cPLA2 for phosphatidylcholine (PC)-enriched membranes.
evidence: This claim is stated in the introduction and represents a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Three Ca2+ ions are coordinated in the PC-bound structural complex.
source: In contrast to the two bound Ca2+ ions reported in the lipid-free structure (Dessen et al., 1999; Perisic et al., 1998), we observed three Ca2+ ions coordinated in the PC-bound structural complex, consistent with the established Ca2+ dependence of membrane interaction by the C2-domain.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The observation of three Ca2+ ions in the PC-bound structural complex is consistent with the established Ca2+ dependence of membrane interaction by the C2-domain.
source: In contrast to the two bound Ca2+ ions reported in the lipid-free structure (Dessen et al., 1999; Perisic et al., 1998), we observed three Ca2+ ions coordinated in the PC-bound structural complex, consistent with the established Ca2+ dependence of membrane interaction by the C2-domain.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data and previous knowledge.

claim: Two of the three bound Ca2+ ions provide bridging interactions between the C2-domain and the DHPC phosphate group.
source: Two of the three bound Ca2+ ions provide bridging interactions between the C2-domain and the DHPC phosphate group, which also interacts directly with Asn65.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The DHPC-binding mode of the cPLA2α C2-domain differs substantially from that of the PKCα C2-domain or the Syt1 C2A-domain bound to phosphatidylserine (PS) or PI(4,5)P2.
source: The DHPC-binding mode of the cPLA2α C2-domain differs substantially from that of the PKCα C2-domain or the Syt1 C2A-domain bound to phosphatidylserine (PS) or PI(4,5)P2, thereby expanding and deepening our knowledge of the lipid-binding mechanisms that are mediated by the C2-domain.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparisons.

claim: The chicken cPLA2α C2-domain is 81% identical and 93% highly conserved in sequence relative to human cPLA2α C2-domain.
source: However, using purified Gallus gallus (chicken) cPLA2α C2-domain (81% identical and 93% highly conserved sequence relative to human) (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), we obtained crystal complexes with 1,2-dihexanoyl-sn-glycero-3-phosphocholine (DHPC) (Figure 1C), enabling structure determination at 2.2 Å resolution (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by sequence alignment data.

claim: The electron density map for the entire C2-domain polypeptide chain is visible except for the N-terminal glycine, a cloning residue artifact.
source: The electron density map for the entire C2-domain polypeptide chain is visible except for the N-terminal glycine, a cloning residue artifact.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by crystallographic data.

claim: Extra electron density corresponding to a bound DHPC molecule is found in the map near the position reported for a bound MES buffer molecule in the structure of full-length human cPLA2α.
source: Notably, extra electron density corresponding to a bound DHPC molecule is found in the map (Figure 1D), near the position reported for a bound MES [2-(N-morpholino) ethanesulfonic acid] buffer molecule in the structure of full-length human cPLA2α (Dessen et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by crystallographic data and comparison with previous structures.

claim: Three C2-domain molecules comprise the asymmetric unit and each C2-domain contains one bound DHPC molecule.
source: Three C2-domain molecules comprise the asymmetric unit and each C2-domain contains one bound DHPC molecule.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by crystallographic data.

claim: The C2-domain–DHPC complex exhibits a β-sandwich topology formed by a pair of four-stranded antiparallel β-sheets.
source: The C2-domain–DHPC complex exhibits a β-sandwich topology formed by a pair of four-stranded antiparallel β-sheets (one formed by the β4, β1, β8 and β7 strands; the other by the β3, β2, β5 and β6 strands) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The structure of the chicken C2-domain with bound DHPC is almost the same as that of human lipid-free form with a small overall root mean square (r.m.s.) deviation of 0.7 Å after superimposition of Cα atoms.
source: The structure of the chicken C2-domain with bound DHPC is almost the same as that of human lipid-freeform (Dessen et al., 1999; Perisic et al., 1998) with a small overall root mean square (r.m.s.) deviation of 0.7 Å after superimposition of Cα atoms (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison data.

claim: Two of the three bound Ca2+ ions in the C2-domain–DHPC complex correspond to the bound Ca1 and Ca4 in lipid-free human protein reported previously.
source: Interestingly, we observed three bound Ca2+ ions in the C2-domain–DHPC complex (Figure 1B, D and E), two of which correspond to the bound Ca1 and Ca4 in lipid-free human protein reported previously (Dessen et al., 1999; Perisic et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data and comparison with previous structures.

claim: The Ca1 ion is bound via side-chain interactions with Asp40, Asp43, Asp93 and Asn95 and the main chain carbonyl group of Ala94.
source: We found that the Ca1 ion is bound via side-chain interactions with Asp40, Asp43, Asp93 and Asn95 and the main chain carbonyl group of Ala94; whereas Ca4 is bound via interaction with the side chains of Asp40, Asp43 and Asn65 and the main-chain carbonyl group of Thr41 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Ca4 is bound via interaction with the side chains of Asp40, Asp43 and Asn65 and the main-chain carbonyl group of Thr41.
source: We found that the Ca1 ion is bound via side-chain interactions with Asp40, Asp43, Asp93 and Asn95 and the main chain carbonyl group of Ala94; whereas Ca4 is bound via interaction with the side chains of Asp40, Asp43 and Asn65 and the main-chain carbonyl group of Thr41 (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The Ca1 and Ca4 coordination networks are almost the same as those in the lipid-free structure.
source: The Ca1 and Ca4 coordination networks are almost the same as those in the lipid-free structure (Dessen et al., 1999; Perisic et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison with previous structures.

claim: Binding of the third Ca2+ involves a stabilizing contact with Asn65 and interaction with the DHPC phosphoryl group.
source: Binding of the third Ca2+ involves a stabilizing contact with Asn65 and interaction with the DHPC phosphoryl group.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The third Ca2+ is designated CaPC because of its novel location at CBL1, which is unique when compared with Ca2+-binding sites in various other C2-domains.
source: This Ca2+ is designated CaPC because of its novel location at CBL1, which is unique when compared with Ca2+-binding sites in various other C2-domains (Rizo and Südhof, 1998; Corbalan-Garcia and Gómez-Fernández, 2014).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison with other C2-domains.

claim: The DHPC polar headgroup docks with the CBLs, whereas the fatty acid chains are largely exposed to solvent.
source: The DHPC polar headgroup docks with the CBLs, whereas the fatty acid chains are largely exposed to solvent.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The orientation of bound PC in the complex is consistent with a function as an embedded membrane-anchoring element for the docking site of the protein.
source: This orientation of bound PC in the complex is consistent with a function as an embedded membrane-anchoring element for the docking site of the protein.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is an inference based on the structural data.

claim: The DHPC sn-2 chain is largely disordered except for the ester group.
source: In the C2-domain–DHPC complex (Figure 2B), the DHPC sn-2 chain is largely disordered except for the ester group, but nearly all of the sn-1 chain is observable because of the stabilizing interaction with CaPC and the partial contact by Leu39 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Nearly all of the DHPC sn-1 chain is observable because of the stabilizing interaction with CaPC and the partial contact by Leu39.
source: In the C2-domain–DHPC complex (Figure 2B), the DHPC sn-2 chain is largely disordered except for the ester group, but nearly all of the sn-1 chain is observable because of the stabilizing interaction with CaPC and the partial contact by Leu39 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The DHPC phosphoryl group is positioned at the center of the CBLs, with the -N+(CH3)3 group of DHPC directed towards CBL3.
source: The DHPC phosphoryl group is positioned at the center of the CBLs, with the -N+(CH3)3 group of DHPC directed towards CBL3 (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The phosphoryl group is stabilized mainly by Ca2+-mediated bridging interactions.
source: The phosphoryl group is stabilized mainly by Ca2+-mediated bridging interactions.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The only direct interaction between the phosphoryl group and the C2-domain is a hydrogen bond with the side chain of Asn65 (~3.1 Å).
source: The only direct interaction between the phosphoryl group and the C2-domain is a hydrogen bond with the side chain of Asn65 (~3.1 Å) (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Ca1 does not coordinate with the DHPC molecule.
source: Although Ca1 does not coordinate with the DHPC molecule, Ca4 does interact with two oxygen atoms of the DHPC phosphoryl group in bifurcated fashion (2.1 and 3.7 Å).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Ca4 interacts with two oxygen atoms of the DHPC phosphoryl group in bifurcated fashion (2.1 and 3.7 Å).
source: Although Ca1 does not coordinate with the DHPC molecule, Ca4 does interact with two oxygen atoms of the DHPC phosphoryl group in bifurcated fashion (2.1 and 3.7 Å).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: CaPC bridges the C2-domain to DHPC via its phosphoryl group (3.6 Å) and sn-1 carbonyl group (3.2 Å) and also interacts with the Asn65 side-chain (3.1 Å).
source: CaPC, which was not observed in two previous lipid-free structures (Perisic et al., 1998), bridges the C2-domain to DHPC via its phosphoryl group (3.6 Å) and sn-1 carbonyl group (3.2 Å) and also interacts with the Asn65 side-chain (3.1 Å) (Figure 2; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Ca4 and CaPC mediate both partial charge neutralization of the DHPC phosphoryl group, and by doing so, bridge the C2-domain and PC.
source: Thus, Ca4 and CaPC mediate both partial charge neutralization of the DHPC phosphoryl group, and by doing so, bridge the C2-domain and PC.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is an inference based on structural data.

claim: The -N+(CH3)3 group of DHPC is partially surrounded by Tyr96 of CBL3 and His62 and Asn64 of CBL2.
source: The -N+(CH3)3 group of DHPC is partially surrounded by Tyr96 of CBL3 and His62 and Asn64 of CBL2 (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The Tyr96 aromatic ring stacks in planar-like fashion with the cationic -N+(CH3)3 group.
source: Importantly, the Tyr96 aromatic ring stacks in planar-like fashion with the cationic -N+(CH3)3 group.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: Cation-π interaction occurs at distances of less than 6.0 Å between a positively charged atom or group and the flat face of an aromatic ring that has a partial negative charge due to delocalized π electrons.
source: This kind of electrostatic interaction, that is cation-π interaction, occurs at distances of less than 6.0 Å between a positively charged atom or group and the flat face of an aromatic ring that has a partial negative charge due to delocalized π electrons (Dougherty, 2013; Gallivan and Dougherty, 1999).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous literature defining cation-π interactions.

claim: The position of the -N+(CH3)3 group is further stabilized by van der Waals contacts with the Ala94 methyl group and by a possible weak (off-angle) cation-π interaction with the His62 imidazole ring.
source: The position of the -N+(CH3)3 group is further stabilized by van der Waals contacts with the Ala94 methyl group and by a possible weak (off-angle) cation-π interaction with the His62 imidazole ring (Figure 2B and C).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: The orientation of His62 appears to be affected by hydrogen bonding (2.8 Å) between its imidazole group and the side-chain carbonyl group of Asn64.
source: The orientation of His62 appears to be affected by hydrogen bonding (2.8 Å) between its imidazole group and the side-chain carbonyl group of Asn64, which also interacts (weakly) with the -N+(CH3)3 group.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural data.

claim: In the structure of the lipid-free C2-domain, a cadmium ion from the crystallization buffer was localized between Tyr96 and His62, consistent with cation-π interaction.
source: Notably, in the structure of the lipid-free C2-domain (Perisic et al., 1998), a cadmium ion from the crystallization buffer was localized between Tyr96 and His62, consistent with cation-π interaction (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by comparison with previous structural data.

claim: Previous mutational analyses support His62 interaction with PC as well as a more significant role for this residue in binding C1P.
source: Previous mutational analyses support His62 interaction with PC as well as a more significant role for this residue in binding C1P (Ward et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: In other proteins that specifically bind PC, such as the PC transfer protein, cation–π interactions involving Tyr and Trp are determinants of PC specificity.
source: In other proteins that specifically bind PC, such as the PC transfer protein, cation–π interactions involving Tyr and Trp are determinants of PC specificity (Roderick et al., 2002; Kang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DHPC binding induced no major conformational changes in the C2-domain CBLs.
source: In our study, DHPC binding induced no major conformational changes in the C2-domain CBLs.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by structural comparison data.

claim: NMR studies of the cPLA2α C2-domain depict the Tyr96 indole ring in an outward position when not interacting with dodecylphosphocholine micelles.
source: Notably, NMR studies of the cPLA2α C2-domain depict the Tyr96 indole ring in an outward position when not interacting with dodecylphosphocholine micelles (Xu et al., 1998).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: PC binding could require local conformational changes, such as inward flipping of Tyr96, to optimize π–cation interaction for complex formation.
source: Thus, PC binding could require local conformational changes, such as inward flipping of Tyr96, to optimize π–cation interaction for complex formation.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and is a speculation based on comparison with NMR data.

claim: The Y96A point mutant exhibited significantly reduced affinity for PC bilayer vesicles when compared to either the conservatively mutated Y96F or the control C2–domain, as shown by SPR.
source: The Y96A point mutant, which is unable to undergo cation–π interaction with the -N+(CH3)3 group of DHPC, exhibited significantly reduced affinity for PC bilayer vesicles when compared to either the conservatively mutated Y96F (which supports strong cation-π interaction) or the control C2–domain, as shown by SPR (Figure 3A; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by SPR data.

claim: Disruption of the PC phosphate group interaction with N65 by point mutation to Asp (N65D) significantly reduced partitioning to PC vesicles.
source: Also, disruption of the PC phosphate group interaction with N65 by point mutation to Asp (N65D) significantly reduced partitioning to PC vesicles (Figure 3A; Table 1).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by SPR data.

claim: In previous surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and DHPC-coated bead studies involving a refolded C2-domain containing a 20-residue affinity tag including 6xHis, weaker affinity of Y96A and D65A mutants for DHPC was observed.
source: In previous surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and DHPC-coated bead studies involving a refolded C2-domain containing a 20-residue affinity tag including 6xHis (Bittova et al., 1999; Stahelin and Cho, 2001b; Ward et al., 2012), weaker affinity of Y96A and D65A mutants for DHPC was observed.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The need for greater Ca2+ concentrations to induce Y96A or N65D partitioning to the PC model membranes compared to either Y96F or control C2-domain partitioning, was clearly evident.
source: The need for greater Ca2+ concentrations to induce Y96A or N65D partitioning to the PC model membranes compared to either Y96F or control C2-domain partitioning, was clearly evident.
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by FRET data.

claim: The association of the Y96A mutant with PAPC-containing mixed micelles is significantly reduced compared to that of either the conservative Y96F point mutant or the control enzyme.
source: Notably, the data support the functional importance of Tyr96 for PC association. Specifically, the association of the Y96A mutant with PAPC-containing mixed micelles is significantly reduced, that is , the dissociation rate is increased as signified by an increased KsA, compared to that of either the conservative Y96F point mutant or the control enzyme (Figure 3E; Table 2).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by activity assay data.

claim: The turnover of the Y96A mutant enzyme displayed allosteric sigmoidal kinetics once the enzyme was bound to the surface of micelles containing PAPC without significantly affecting K0.5.
source: Also, the turnover of the Y96A mutant enzyme displayed allosteric sigmoidal kinetics once the enzyme was bound to the surface of micelles containing PAPC (e.g., a significant difference in Vmax was observed) without significantly affecting K0.5(i.e., the PAPC concentration that produces half-maximal enzyme velocity) (Figure 3F; Table 3).
evidence: This claim is stated in the results section and supported by activity assay data.

claim: Tyr96 is key for recognizing and binding PC in the membrane but not for the enzymatic activity of the catalytic domain towards substrate once the enzyme is associated with the membrane.
source: These data indicate that Tyr96 is key for recognizing and binding PC in the membrane but not for the enzymatic activity of the catalytic domain towards substrate once the enzyme is associated with the membrane.
